name: North Carolina
summary_text: North Carolina is a state within the United States, and a trans visitor stands under the federal framework before any state rule applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The same order required federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender," mandated removal of materials promoting what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. The facilities bar reaches federal buildings in North Carolina.  The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker had been available since 2022. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the restriction remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.  Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued on 5 February 2025, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.  Gender-affirming care is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described such care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.  Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.  Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.  Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.  At state level, facility rules are the defining North Carolina question. After the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance in March 2016 allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the North Carolina General Assembly met in emergency session and passed House Bill 2, which barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people and required people to use public bathrooms corresponding with the sex listed on their birth certificate. The law drew global backlash, with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called it "state-sponsored discrimination" and sued, while North Carolina filed its own suit. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017 in the face of the boycotts.  Facility use remains an active legislative subject in North Carolina. In the 2025 session Republican lawmakers were again pushing a transgender bathroom bill, years after the HB 2 boycotts forced the repeal, so a visitor should expect facilities access to be contested rather than settled.  Lethal violence against trans people in North Carolina does not track the state's protective posture. A July 2026 investigative data analysis comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring records found that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women; its state rate chart places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women, on a recorded base of three or more victims that the analysis acknowledges is an undercount, and characterises the state as moderate-risk. That rating describes recorded killings and should not be read as an assurance of safety for an individual visitor.

name: North Dakota
summary_text: North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.  North Dakota law independently closes the document route that a trans visitor may rely on at the state level. The 2023 statute tracked by the Movement Advancement Project bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery. The tracker marks North Dakota a negative law state, and a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than applies in many other states. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal-risk assessment built from five years of daily legislative tracking places North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, a rule that forces trans people to out themselves when showing documents. The same assessment records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.  Facilities access is restricted across a growing group of states: a Movement Advancement Project tally counts bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity elsewhere, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Screening inside the country carries an outing risk of its own, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy; several foreign governments have responded, with advisories about trans people travelling to the United States issued from April 2025 and at least eight European countries adjusting entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens by March 2025.
